core: Working definition of leadership, attributed: the process of guiding and motivating others toward the achievement of organizational goals (OpenStax 6.4); everyday shorthand: the ability to influence and guide people toward a goal.
A leader can be anyone in an organization, regardless of position, able to influence others to act or follow, often by their own choice (OpenStax 6.4).

Leadership versus management: influence and direction versus coordination and process; managers are designated leaders by structure but may rely on position or coercion; management is a sibling topic, reference only.
Four leadership styles named with one line each and when each fits: autocratic, democratic (participative), laissez-faire (free rein), and transformational.
What leaders do: set direction, motivate, build trust, and model behavior, each named with one line.
Leadership is situational: no single style works everywhere; effective leaders match the style to the maturity and competency of the people doing the tasks (OpenStax 6.4; CFI).
Can leadership be learned: the general answer, stated simply, is yes, skills and habits can be developed and practiced.
Honest framing: leadership is demonstrated, not declared; a title does not make someone a leader.
supporting: Leadership styles as a behavioral approach leaders use to influence, motivate, and direct followers (CFI).
The degree to which a style builds follower trust is a major tenet of its effectiveness (CFI).
Leadership style as a continuum of authority: leader-centered (autocratic) to group-centered (free rein), with participative in between (OpenStax 6.4, Table 6.4).
outOfScope: Management depth (functions, managerial roles, managerial skills, planning/organizing/controlling detail) — owned by the management topic.
Organizational structure and reporting lines — owned by organizational-structure.
Motivation theories and power-base frameworks in depth — owned by the management topic.
Company case studies of named leaders — general concepts only, all examples original.
Personality psychology of leadership traits — the lesson states only the general answer that skills can be developed.

claims.claim: Leadership is the process of guiding and motivating others toward the achievement of organizational goals (the working definition used in this lesson, attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Business).
A leader can be anyone in an organization, regardless of position, able to influence others to act or follow, often by their own choice.

Managers are designated leaders according to the organizational structure, but may need to use negative consequences or coercion to achieve change; authority from position differs from leadership influence.

Management is the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals, based on four functional areas: planning, organizing, leading, and controlling.
Leadership styles can be placed on a continuum encompassing autocratic, participative (democratic, consensual, consultative), and free-rein (laissez-faire) styles.

Autocratic leaders make decisions with little input and expect detailed instructions to be followed; democratic leaders share decision-making and encourage discussion; laissez-faire leaders turn over authority and freedom to the group.
Transformational leadership transforms a business or group by inspiring team members to raise their bar and achieve what they did not think they were capable of.
No leadership style is effective all the time; effective leaders use situational leadership, selecting a style that matches the maturity and competency levels of the people completing the tasks.

No one leadership style fits all organizations or situations; there is no one right way to lead, and leaders may need to switch between styles depending on factors such as the type of work and the experience of the team.
The degree to which a leadership style builds follower trust is a major tenet of its effectiveness; followers who trust their leader are more likely to follow through with instructions.

Leadership styles are behavioral approaches used to influence, motivate, and direct followers, and leaders can understand their own style and determine how to be more effective, which supports the general answer that leadership behaviors and skills can be developed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many leadership styles are there?
positions: OpenStax Introduction to Business presents three styles on a continuum: autocratic, participative, and free-rein (laissez-faire).

Corporate Finance Institute lists democratic, autocratic, laissez-faire, and transformational as common styles, with additional styles (transactional, servant, coach, charismatic, strategic) beyond them.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four styles named in the topic brief: the three classic continuum styles from OpenStax plus transformational from CFI, each with one line and a general sense of when it fits, and notes that style lists vary across sources.

positions: Trait-based views historically treated leadership qualities as largely innate personal characteristics.
Behavioral views, reflected in CFI's framing of styles as behavioral approaches and its advice that leaders can understand their own style and become more effective, treat leadership as developable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the honest general answer, stated simply: leadership involves skills and habits that can be developed and practiced, while acknowledging that some people find it more natural than others. Trait-psychology depth is out of scope.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No machine-generated draft existed for this topic; every claim was sourced during this research pass. The brief's framing that leadership is demonstrated, not declared is used as the honest framing, consistent with the OpenStax statement that a leader can be anyone regardless of position.
correctionsNeeded: Kept the leadership-versus-management distinction to a single subsection and deferred management depth to the sibling management topic.
Attributed the working definition to OpenStax Introduction to Business 6.4 in the lesson, vocabulary, and evidence claims.
Kept all examples original (food truck, barista, warehouse supervisor, senior design studio, restaurant kitchen, hiking guide, committee, study group, volunteer crew); none taken from the sources.
Named all four required styles with one line each and stated the situational note that no style works everywhere.
